About two-thirds through the game, a thought hit me: "I'm not playing a game; I'm having an experience." That’s exactly what God of War is, an experience. The graphics, setting, lore, gameplay, set-pieces, voice acting, emotions, and story are all fantastic.

As a father who has experienced the loss of a child, Kratos’ grief resonated deeply with me. I felt his struggle to bond with Atreus, the fear of watching your child go astray, and the pride in witnessing their growth. Faye’s pain also struck a chord with the relentless need to protect your child, no matter the cost. The story doesn’t rush these emotions. Instead, it gives the characters time to fully process their grief, leading to a powerful and satisfying conclusion.

Beyond the emotional depth, the gameplay is exhilarating. The combat is fluid and responsive, making each battle feel dynamic and rewarding. Facing the dragon and the intense fights with the Stranger were especially epic. By the end, I felt like an unstoppable force.

I never played the previous God of War games, but I never felt lost. The story provided everything I needed to know, which I greatly appreciated.

This game is an absolute gem, and I can’t wait to experience Ragnarok when it arrives on PC.

On another note I so how much less action packed God of War has become, but it is expected due to a change of the type of game it has become. [h3][b]God of War[/b][/h3]

After finishing the main story, I can pretty confidently say that God of War turned out much better than I expected. Goin' in, I mostly thought of it as 'nother game about Kratos killing gods, just with a new setting and a different look. Instead it ended up being a really strong reboot of the series – and one with much more emotional depth than I expected from God of War in general.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3369330496

The biggest change is obviously Kratos himself. The older games were mostly about rage, revenge and destroying EVERYTHING in his path while this one is much more focused on remorse, redemption and dealing with the past. The relationship between Kratos and Atreus is basically the center of the whole story and I think Santa Monica handled it reallyy well. It develops gradually, without trying too hard to force emotional moments every few minutes. The story stayed interesting from beginning to end, and I never really reached a point where I wanted to drop the game or take a long break(or break in general) from it.

The presentation is also still impressive. GoW looks great even compared to much newer games, and the art direction does a lot of the work here. The different locations/creatures/environments all have their own style while still feeling like parts of the same world. The soundtrack and overall sound design fit the game just as well, especially during the bigger fights and story moments.

Gameplay-wise I think the game holds up very well, even if it isnt perfect. Combat is fairly easy to understand but there's enough depth in the weapons, abilities and different attacks to keep it interesting. It can feel epic without becoming overly complicated, which I appreciated. Throwing and recalling the Leviathan Axe also never really gets old – it’s just satisfying.

That said, there is definitely some repetition. Enemy variety could be better, and after a while you start seeing familiar enemies and similar encounters more often than youd like. Some bosses also reuse the same basic ideas. It’s noticeable, especially later in the game, but I never felt like it became bad enough to seriously damage the experience. The combat itself is enjoyable enough to carry most of those repeated encounters.

I also like that the game gives you enough things to do outside the main path without making the world feel overloaded. Exploration, side quests and optional fights are there if you want them, but the game doesn't constantly throw markers at you from every direction. It helps keep the focus on the story while still giving you reasons to look around.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2925853587

Overall, God of War is absolutely worth playin'. It takes a series that was known mostly for brutal action and turns it into something much more character-focused without losing what made Kratos interesting in the first place.

It deserved the praise it got – although personally, I still wouldn't put it above RDR2 for GOTY. Still, if youve ever thought about trying it, I'd definitely give it a shot

This game [i]officially[/i] gets the award for being the game that I never thought I would love. I have a bit of a bias and usually prefer female protagonist based games, so I have avoided this one for years. I’m a cozy gamer, and there is nothing cozy about Kratos lol. Can't always judge a book by its cover tho, because this has hands down become my favourite action-adventure game. 

It’s the father and son interactions throughout the game that completely won me over. I was expecting a brutish, cold hearted, stoic character whom I would hate. And whilst he is some of those things, I particularly found myself drawn to Kratos's honesty and blunt nature. While he may not show it in conventional ways, you can tell he loves his son as he tries to guide and train him throughout the game. You get to witness the growth of the relationship between him and "boy", awkward moments and all. I found myself living for the scenes when Kratos would share more about himself with his son, esp story telling time on the boat.

The story and combat are equally engaging. I thought I was walking into a hack and slash but there is the most perfect balance between fighting, lore/exploration and puzzles. You fight as Kratos but his son is there as an active sidekick, and you get to build on both of their toolkits. I love how you aren't overwhelmed with side quests and filler. There is never a dull moment or that feeling of stale repetitiveness. You can adjust the difficulty as needed and it plays very well on the deck. 

Just all around top notch gaming. 

I have never ran so fast to a steam sale in all my life for the second installment. Even if it wasn't on sale, I was picking it up. Really hoping for remakes of the original so I can experience how it all started *fingers crossed*

Update: I usually hate side quests but there is extensive lore and backstory to uncover by exploring the map. You get so much dialogue by travelling on the Lake of Nine, it’s actually becoming my favourite part of the game. Peak exploring experience!!

God of War is one of my favorite game franchises and I'm glad to being finally able to play this masterpiece on PC. It was the summer of 2007 when we first discovered God of War with my brother and cousin on a PS2 demo disc that my cousin possessed. It was God of War 2 and the game left us speechless even though we were far too young to be playing such a violent game but just like all the children back then, we didn't care. We kept playing until we finished the demo. Naturally, we asked my uncle to bring us the full game and luckily for us, he did! Now we had the full God of War 2 experience on our hands but we didn't have a memory card to save our progress. Once again, that didn't stop us. After 6 hours of gaming, we conquered the game and the cliffhanger left us both excited and frustrated. We later asked my uncle to bring us the first game and we successfully finished that one and put an end to Ares as well. We somehow found a way to play God of War 3 afterwards and managed to beat it as well. Knowing there wouldn't be a God of War 4, we resorted playing PSP titles and even the official java game called God of War: Betrayal. Years later, 2016 shone bright upon us. Santa Monica delivered a gameplay video of the new God of War which took place in Norse Mythology. Not gonna lie, seeing Blades of Chaos not being present in game, we were quite disappointed and this new style didn't appeal to us. We tried to hate this game for what it is. Until one day my cousin bought it for his PS4 and we were brought back to our childhood once again. We were greeted with a more mature Kratos this time. It's like he grew up as we grew up. It took some time but the game grew on us. We learned to appreciate the change and embraced it fully. Now we pre-ordered Ragnarok and simply cannot wait for it! 

Leaving my own past behind, let's get to God of War. Kratos ended the Greek pantheon and made his way to Nordic shores to live as a man rather than a god. He found himself a wife, and a son followed soon after. Being distant from his son and losing his wife at an unfortunate time, he finds himself alone with his boy. Through the game, you'll get to see the development of the relationship of Kratos with his son on their journey to scatter his wife's ashes from the highest peak in all realms. Kratos is no saint. He's one of the worst examples of a horrendous human being. However, despite lacking necessary humanity towards others, Kratos always deeply cared about his family. He's aware that this is his chance to make things right with his previous family and find inner peace he's sought after. God of War manages to turn such a simple story to a deep, meaningful one. It shows that it is not goal that makes the journey worthwhile, but how you get there.

The gameplay-wise, it's very good. Unlike the previous games, this one gives player a free camera at their command and adds lots of RPG elements, thus resulting in exploration being very rewarding and satisfying. On the other hand, combat is great. You have this Leviathan Axe with lots of moves and variety and you get to use your good old pals Blades of Chaos. They are a bit weird to use from a third person point of view but I eventually got used to it, I'm sure you will as well. However, Leviathan Axe feels more powerful overall therefore I ended up using it more than Blades of Chaos. All good things aside, there aren't much enemy variety in it and most of them are overused through the game. I think this is the only bad thing I can say about this game but I'm sure Ragnarok will change that. From a completionist perspective, this game was surprisingly fun to 100%. Sigrun gave me a hard time on Give Me God of War difficulty, though. Don't get me wrong, I'm not complaining. She's perfectly designed as a challenging boss fight and she was probably the toughest boss I've ever faced in any game. Props to Santa Monica for that. 

Moving onto another topic, as you all know, God of War has won the GOTY award back in 2018 and most people opposed it by saying that Red Dead Redemption 2 was the one that deserved that award instead of God of War. As a diehard God of War fan and not having played Red Dead Redemption 2 yet, I slightly agree with this mostly because how very well detailed Red Dead Redemption 2 is. Like I said, I'm stating a sketchy opinion here because I've yet to play Red Dead Redemption 2. Will this change after I've experienced the game? We'll see. Anyway, just wanted to mention this here since we have been discussing this topic with my friends since 2018. 

[h1]TL;DR[/h1]
God of War is an emotional journey of a man who's having trouble facing his past. From narrative to gameplay, it delivers the best of them. I believe that this game should be experienced by every human being out there.

As a fan of the God of War franchise, this game was truly an amazing experience and is definitely one of the best games I've played.

The story: The story is a beautiful one. Kratos and his BOY Atreus set out on a journey to scatter the ashes of Atreus' mother Faye, at her dying request. This journey isn't as straightforward, as they are hunted by the Nordic gods, for reasons that become clear in the game. The story sees the growth of the father-son relationship, Kratos as an outsider who wants to put his past life behind, the growth of Atreus as a Warrior God and also the development towards a certain famed Nordic event, that will be revealed in the game.

The characters: The lead characters Kratos and Atreus have been depicted quite well, with their words and action always in line with their developing personalities. The side characters are a delight especially Mimir and the dwarves.

The combat: This is possibly my favorite part of the game. Due to the new camera which is just behind the shoulder of Kratos, each fight feels much more visceral. Unlike the previous installments in the franchise, combat here is strategic and requires planning. The weapon, skill and gear upgrades are all different and hence can be tailored according to the fighting style of the player, which I found particularly useful.

The visuals: Graphics in this game are an experience. The detail in the world and characters is breathtaking and really adds to the overall gaming experience.

Certainly a generation defining game, and definitely one of the greatest games I've ever played.

God of War is worth your time if you like a good story with great characters and lore. I'm so impressed by the pacing in this game. If you play on lower difficulties, like I did, the game unfolds like a book, and I mean that with the highest respect. The discoveries, plot twists, and character development are done so well, it's just something you don't see often in video games. 
God of War also does something really special, it makes you a dad, and I also mean that with the highest respect. You have a kid throughout the whole game, and you are his protector, and teacher. You are also a God, and you're a flawed father that has just lost his wife, the boys mother. The emotional strings throughout this game are the highlights for me. Its difficult to make a hack and slash, it almost impossible to make a hack and slash with emotional relationships that are done so well, you can't help but care. 

The Good:
The writing and story line are greats. A simple task of spreading your mothers ashes from the highest peak turns into a sprawling adventure and bonding experience with your son. One-liners are funny, and witty, and when you're son is in danger, you can hear it in Kratos' voice. This game is great at invoking emotion. 

Side quests are well done, without being overwhelming. One in particular, the Valkyries, are side bosses that are difficult, much more difficult than the original game bosses. I also enjoy the two worlds that are basically just arenas. I also appreciate the treasure maps, and trinkets you can find scattered around the map. Speaking of map, it's a great size for a game like this, enough without zones for the sake of zones. 

Some customization with weapons, armor, and skills, and again, not overwhelming amounts, which fits perfect for a game like this.  

Bosses are larger than life, and sound amazing. All the voice acting in this game is top-notch. All the sound in this game is crisp. The attention to detail is definitely there.

The Bad:
I only have one real negative critique of this game, the combat. I dropped the difficulty pretty early in this game because I kept getting killed from monsters I wasn't facing, or by moves I didn't understand. The camera during combat is not perfect, and the mobs always seem to use a move I'd never seen before that would do take most of my health bar. I usually like to play action RPGs on the highest difficulty but it was just too frustrating with this game. Combat felt too random at times. 

Other than that, I completely admit these next few are nit-picking. 

Why do I have to travel through a dimension to get to another way-gate? Fast travel is essential in this game, like most games that allow it, but in this game you have to walk through an ethereal world for a few minutes every time you want to fast-travel? Why? I never understood what that was supposed to add to the game. Just filler time. 

Why does traveling to a different world take a minute too? It's cool the first time, but I had to travel to different worlds quite a few times, I didn't need the lights and the roots song-and-dance every time, sort of just felt like a way to fill a few minutes. 

Puzzles are done fine in this game, I just don't like puzzles in general as a game mechanic, and there are a lot of them in God of War. There were a few times I got stuck and had to run around in circles for a while, but to the games credit, It does have a tracker that tells you if there is something you need in the area, or tells you where to go to continue the main quest line. 

That's all I have to say. Buy this game, it's worth your time. I'm a little late to the party with this one but it lived up to the hype.

[h1]Introduction[/h1]
With [b]Sony[/b] finally bringing their IPs to PC, a [b]God of War (GoW)[/b] game is playable for the first time on PC. This is the first [b]GoW[/b] game that I have played, however, this one does not require you to have played the previous games in order to understand the story. This game will feature gods from [b]Norse Mythology[/b] and it’s rich with it. This makes the feeling of being in the world really fitting, something that I myself like.

[h1]Pros and Cons[/h1]
[b]Pros[/b]
[list]
[*]The story is really well done, with lots of lore scattered around
[*]Fun and very interesting characters with their own personalities
[*]Combat is engaging, with interesting upgrades to utilize
[*]Awesome boss battles that are really fun
[*]Many secrets to acquire to upgrade your health, rage, weapons, or armor
[*]Amazing graphics that are very nice to look at
[/list]

[b]Cons[/b]
[list]
[*][b]Alfheim[/b] felt a little slow when I first arrived in the area
[*][b]Kratos[/b] will only use his fists during Spartan Rage and won’t use any of his weapons
[/list]

[h1]Story[/h1]
Many years have passed since [b]Kratos[/b] took his revenge on the [b]Olympian gods[/b] and him having survived the final battle with [b]Zeus[/b]. [b]Kratos[/b] has since traveled to [b]Midgard[/b] in [b]Ancient Norway[/b], where he now lives with his son [b]Atreus[/b]. They are both mourning the passing of [b]Faye[/b], [b]Kratos[/b] second wife, and her final request was for her ashes to be spread from the highest peak of the [b]Nine Realms[/b]. [b]Joseph Seed[/b] from [b]Far Cry 5[/b], who is a mysterious stranger in this game, attacks [b]Kratos[/b] at his home and apparently cannot feel any sort of pain. After the fight, [b]Kratos[/b] takes [b]Atreus[/b] and heads out on an adventure, where he will teach his son how to survive a harsh world.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2757653760
The story for [b]God of War[/b] is really good and I honestly think it’s one of the best stories that I have witnessed in gaming. The characters are all brimming with personalities that make them unique and special. My favorite character has to be [b]Mimir[/b], he is funny, has lots of knowledge and wisdom, while being a travel comparing. 

I also like [b]Sindri[/b] and [b]Brok[/b], who are both dwarfs, as they help upgrade weapons and much more, because they are blacksmiths. [b]Sindri[/b] is an extreme germaphobe and I can kind of somewhat relate to him. I mean, I am not putting my hands in a dragon's mouth to grab a tooth. [b]Brok[/b], who is my favorite out of the two brothers, is a hothead who has a very serious-like attitude, with a great voice.

There are other supporting characters that are really good too with their own unique personalities that are honestly worth talking about. However, that would make this review longer than it should be.

There is also a ton of lore out there for you to collect and find, each will give you some backstories of some characters or of the areas you visit. 

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Combat is really engaging and fun. I like how the combos worked when attacking enemies. Instead of a top-down perspective similar to games like [b]Devil May Cry[/b], it takes a third-person camera, where you are right behind [b]Kratos[/b]. Despite this being my first [b]God of War game[/b], this gameplay change works very well and as mentioned before is really fun.

You will start out the game using [b]Leviathan’s Axe[/b] which has ice-based powers that can be recalled at any time when thrown and is also used for puzzle solving. My favorite weapon out of the two has to be [b]The Blades of Chaos[/b], these are fire-based swords that can attack multiple enemies. Each of these weapons can be upgraded and have enchantments to them, which can provide stat bonuses or unique perks when it is selected and equipped. 

Armor can also be upgraded and have up to three enchantment sockets to them. There are also upgrades that you can get from getting EXP, these can give you extra attacks of other special abilities.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2757654577
[b]Atreus[/b] also has a few upgrades that he can get as well, like extra arrow damage and can get access to light and shock arrows. Light arrows can weaken enemies and stun them while lighting arrows shock and paralyze them. [b]Atreus[/b] can even help you in combat and help solve some puzzles, he is actually quite useful and not someone who is just there as a character. 

There are some amazing bosses that you can go and fight, they are challenging and that’s what makes a boss fight legendary. My favorite fight has to be [b]Hraezlyr[/b], a dragon that can shoot lightning from its mouth. The fight was just outright fun and satisfying after beating it, though there are other great bosses throughout the game, and they do keep the hype up. 

Kratos can enter a rage mode if his rage meter is at a certain length, if you played [b]Devil May Cry[/b] and know about [b]Dante’s Devil Trigger[/b], think of it like that. [b]Kratos[/b] gets increased attack damage and life steal when in this mode, it’s best used when you are in a sticky situation.

There are also a ton of secrets for you to find, some of them are upgrades to your weapons or armor, while some are for your health and rage meter. The game rewards you for going out of your way to finding things and is something that I myself really like.

There are two issues that I have with [b]God of War[/b]. Now, I should note that these may be nitpicky to some. The first issue that I had was that I felt when I entered [b]Alfheim[/b], the game just seemed to slow down in terms of story. I guess moving all of these giant gemstones really killed it for me. The next issue will have to do with [b]Kratos[/b] entering his rage mode. For some reason, [b]Kratos[/b] will only use his fists in this state. Even with all of that combat knowledge, he never seemed to have made any attacks with [b]Leviathan’s Axe[/b] or [b]The Blades of Chaos[/b].

[h1]In-Depth[/h1]
[h3]Father and Son[/h3]
Kratos retired from a lifetime of battle and moved to Midgard, among the myth and legends of Norse folklore. The recent passing of his wife marks a critical moment in the insofar stern, cold relationship he has with his son Atreus, trained from infancy to follow the disciplined ways of his father despite his gentler heart; their relation is the pivotal point of the whole story. They must journey to the highest mountain to give the final farewell to their beloved - a task easier said than done, since Midgard is a land fraught with peril, home to cursed creatures and deadly magic. This setting is masterfully realized, both visually and lore-wise, with plenty of real references and lore about Norse gods, monsters and tales of old - of course it's still a videogame, so expect some "poetical licenses" - that make it all the more spectacular, though. Between damp caves, ancient ruins and even entirely different planes of existence, their journey will never be dull or uninteresting.

[h3]To the Nine Realms and Beyond[/h3]
After a rather linear early game section, the duo will be able to explore Midgard freely, with the enormous Lake of Nine acting as a central hub towards several side areas. The map structure is semi-open world, with the very topography changing and opening previously inaccessible areas as certain story events unfold. Exploring is interesting, and brings a bounty of rewards often barred behind fights or puzzles: tough optional encounters, plentiful hidden chests, lore-related artifacts and more than a couple secret areas. Barring a couple instances, players are free to clear the main story at their own pace, and see most side content beforehand if they want to - borderline mandatory at higher difficulties, anyway. In many cases, backtracking once you're stronger or have acquired certain items will be necessary, in a metroidvania-like style of progression as far as optional content is concerned.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2731162070

[h3]Rusty, But Not Rusted Out[/h3]
Both protagonists will be able to improve with two systems of progression, based on gear and XP alike. The former is gained from treasures, bosses, side-quests or crafted at a blacksmith using the materials gained from your adventures, then upgraded to unlock its true potential, mostly in the form of sockets for enchantments, which grant passive abilities and stats. The latter, XP, is gained from enemies and quests and used to purchase skills for Kratos and Atreus, enabling new combos, moves, combat feats and ways to deal with the enemy. Not only that, but XP can also be used to upgrade Runes, powerful spells equipped in each weapon that have a variety of unique effects, and will prove invaluable to fight the harder or more numerous foes.

Combat itself is fast-paced, mostly based on combos and on learning enemy weaknesses to certain elements, damage types while also memorizing their patterns of attack. Atreus and Kratos will work in an increasingly effective synergy, with the former being a support character using arrows, spells and the occasional melee move to aid his father. The enemy variety is good for the most part, and they hurt like hell too on higher difficulties, too bad the mini and optional bosses are heavily recycled and become stale soon enough. Between parries, blocks, dodges and finishers, spells and many different combos, there is enough mechanical variety for the combat to stay fresh until the end regardless.

[h3]A Whole Can of Butt Kicking[/h3]
After clearing the story, there will be a sizable quantity of post-endgame content to clear, however not all of it is of the same quality. The Trials of Musplheim will have a set of 16 challenges each with unique modifiers or rules, like time limits or immortal enemies, that reward unique, powerful materials to make some of the best armors around. Niflheim, the realm of cursed mist, will have a roguelike-style labyrinth that constantly shifts, alongside a time limit: Kratos will have to get out alive in time, with as much loot as he can carry, or lose it all - I found this one to be tremendously grindy and boring, other than badly designed due to excessive RNG dependency. Last but not least the nine Valkyries compose the toughest bosses available, although several of them are half-recycled or copied from others, and the last one of them is more frustrating than enjoyable to fight against. Rewards are great in all cases, but sometimes not worth the pain.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2732723091

[h3]Even Gods Aren't Perfect[/h3]
Both in early and late game the enemy scaling is totally off balance, resulting in overly-spongy foes that take literally dozens of hits, or careful kicking down cliffs when possible, to be defeated, while Kratos even with some of the best armor will die in just a couple of hits. The penalty for having inferior levels compared to an enemy is massive in terms of damage dealt and received, this can make some fights very annoying. The fact fast travel is one-way only until much later on forces unnecessary waste of time through already seen places, this coupled with a high amount of unskippable transition animations makes going anywhere quite a slog for a good while. Also, prepare pen and paper as a good number of "come back later" locations, chests and POIs won't be marked on your map, making it hard to remember them. The bare-handed fight style, unless in specific contexts, proves totally useless and is just worse than using a weapon, it has no place in the combat system 90% of the time and feels like a pointless addition.

[h1]Remember Boy, with great power comes great responsibility.[/h1]

Damn! It really is happening, isn’t it? Kratos is finally on Steam, and even though more Sony games are coming at a slow but sure pace, I can’t stop feeling that this is kind of crazy, I’m not going to talk too much about this because I’m sure I will mention this again once Uncharted is out but, this feels almost unbelievable,anyway, let’s talk about God of War (2018) and why it’s a big deal for me, it’s worth your time and money? Let's find out.

I must start saying I was not a big fan of the Greek saga, it never “clicked” on me and that’s why I never cared about it, however, when this was announced I saw enough changes to make me feel interested on the project but unfortunately I never jumped into it on console for one reason or another, but here we are and now I can finally say what I think about this half-sequel and half-reboot so let’s get this thing started.

Many years have passed since Kratos killed all the Olympians and arrived to northern lands where he formed a new family and started a new peaceful life, however our story begins when his wife dies and Kratos and his son, Atreus, must start a journey to fulfil a promise, however, this journey won’t be easy and they will face perils that will, once again, test Kratos but this time will also test his son, a journey through the nordic realms has started.

While this game makes direct references to the Greek saga, you don’t have to play those in order to enjoy this game as it’s both a direct sequel but also a soft-reboot that is pointing in a new direction for this specific saga, that being said, is the story worth your time?

Story is fundamentally similar to what happened in the Greek saga, Kratos will end up fighting gods and creatures from said mythology, however, this time we will find an older Kratos that acts completely different when facing conflict,  a Kratos that wants to teach his son and strengthen their bound, which is the main topic in this adventure. Game is long but that’s something understandable for two reasons, first of all, the journey itself and all that throws at you: new mythology, characters. In general there’s a lot of new stuff to explore and it sure has the time needed to properly do it. Secondly, Kratos and Atreus, SSM made sure both characters had enough depth to build a more familiar narrative inside the main story which is a very interesting perspective as it’s the foundation for what it’s about to come in the future. Is Atreus ready to be a god? Is Kratos ready to talk about his past? Game will explore all these things and give us answers to those questions . One thing I like a lot is that this game has really heartwarming scenes like the wine one. It's comforting to see a more human Kratos after knowing all his past and where things are going.

At the end of the experience I thought pacing was good and all characters had what they deserved, main and secondary characters, all of them had their respective screen time and most importantly, from a personal point of view, the story is very appealing and makes this entry something completely different than its predecessors, where they failed, this one succeeded.

SSM not only nailed it with the story but also with visuals, it’s just STUNNING! A lot of people consider this as one of the best looking games from the PS4 catalog and trust me, this isn’t different on PC, it’s impressive and truly shows how far gaming has gone in terms of visuals.

God of War 2018 is easily one of the most ambitious games they have done, much like Naughty Dog, SSM has always been a top tier studio with their products. Environments, combats and set-pieces that are mind blowing and GOW '18 is no exception.

From Midgard to Jötunheim, we will visit both decadent but beautiful and vibrant Nordic realms, from a colourful and full of life forest to rusty and decaying structures, detritus from a past era. The level of detail is absolutely spectacular too. In general I would say that, if you like Norsen style, this game will be delightful for you at a visual level, it’s impressive.

Another amazing aspect of this game is the set-pieces and there are quite a few in here. I LOVE them because they usually are the most impressive moments. Sure they aren’t that interactive but in combination with the situation in place, well, truly jaw-dropping moments and very spectacular.

You know what’s also impressive? Music and sound design, so let’s talk about that one because there’s quite a lot to discuss in here too.

One of my favourite things from this title is the soundtrack. It makes you feel that something big is really happening around us with entities that are superior beings. McCreary has a very distinctive touch for this kind of scale of things and the orchestral choices are absolutely sublime for this action, let’s take “The Stranger” theme, starts slow and becomes something massive overtime, HOW AMAZING!

Chorus and orchestra are something that I always appreciate in products like this, nothing like kicking a god’s ass while a whole orchestra in crescendo is accompanying the moment.

But of course Soundtrack isn’t all here, sound design is something that I really love when done correctly and GOW sure does have some stunning moments, as a practical example we have Jörmungandr, the world serpent, his voice echoes like a mountain because he’s the size of a few mountains together, the sound of the beasts is something absolutely fantastic, perhaps this is my inner love for strong sounds in big creatures so it’s delightful to experience it on any game and this one is no exception.

That being said I think it’s about time we jump straight into the most important element of God of War, gameplay loop. It's something that was controversial when it was shown at first but as you will see, doubts quickly disappeared because this system is very interesting and deep.

Firstly, Game was played with KB+M and it was really nice.

Something that might surprise you is that Kratos can no longer jump, that’s right, all actions like jumping or climbing are semi-automatic and camera position is different compared to the original games, however, while at first you will probably think it’s slower and less exciting let me tell you that things get interesting overtime, once you unlock [spoiler]the blades of Chaos[/spoiler], numberless runes and get used to the combat system you will find it very satisfactory.

Upgrading your gear is important as it will unlock movements and that means creating better and more devastating combos, switching weapons from one to another in the middle of a combat will become more and more common and runes applied to those will help you facing different situations as you can change those runes whenever you want, this process might be tedious at first and there are so many potential combinations that it overwhelming and might end up saturating you, however, if you are going to explore how deep is the gameplay loop, this system will be your best ally in the long term.

Let’s not forget about Atreus as it will become more helpful the more we upgrade him too, his arrows can come in handy in certain tricky situations, it won’t win the battles by himself, Atreus is more like a companion turret that will stun enemies and inflict damage to them. By using Kratos combos in combination with Atreus some very spectacular combats might happen, which at the end of the day shows that God of War 2018 is still as brutal and not that different to the original saga in terms of combat and gameplay.

That’s about it, God of War 2018 is worth every penny and every second of your time in my most honest opinion. SSM did an stunning job here and they nailed it with the changes they did, I sure hope you give it a chance and enjoy it as much as I did, even if you are a big fan of the originals or a newcomer I don’t think you will find difficult to enjoy it so here’s hope you have an amazing experience.

The characters and acting are awesome, and later in the game, you will find [spoiler] Mimir, the smartest man alive, who will follow you and tell you so much stories about the world, gods and so on [/spoiler]

Gameplay is amazing. First of all, your main weapon unlike in the previous game is a flying axe. You can throw it literally anywhere you want and call it back. You can upgrade your axe, attach special runes to it, which let you call some kind of magic attacks. What's also new are different armor sets that you can wear, and it wasn't possible to change your armor before. You can also attach some special items to your armor slots which will improve your stats, let you slow down time, and so on. So with your axe combined with all these runes and armors, you can do a lot of different combos, and they are awesome. You will also unlock some other weapon later, but I won't spoil you that. Atreus also helps you in combat a lot. While you are fighting your enemies, he will distract other enemies, and you can order him to shoot arrows and sometimes he will find health gems if you use the correct equipment. He is definitely a big help, and I pretty much spam his arrows all the time. You also have the ability to use rage, in which Kratos is pretty much invulnerable and you will fight using your fists and deal a lot of damage. The rage meter fills up as you are fighting. Camera angles are not as before, they are now zoomed way more and fights are slower in general. Difficulty-wise game is not really hard on normal, but on hard you will need to explore side stuff to be able to overcome your enemies. I didn't even try the hardest difficulty, so I can't say for sure. 

So how's the world and side stuff? Well, the idea was cool, but I think that the execution wasn't the best. As you progress through the main story you will be able to access a few of the nine realms in Norse mythology. Most of the time you will spend in Midgard (the realm of men). While exploring side stuff you will be able to loot a lot of items, track your completion progress, fight strong Valkyries, and do some side quests. I was personally never fan of looting items, finding new gears, and so on, so I didn't really enjoy fighting while exploring. Side quests were pretty boring, so I just did them for completion. Fighting Valkyries was fun, and it was the hardest challenge in the game. I really enjoyed collecting artifacts, finding Odin's ravens, and so on. Aside from Midgard, you will also visit a few more realms, but two of them are just dungeons and combat trials, while 3 are story-related. None of these realms were particularly interesting to me, but they were fine. 

Story bosses are mediocre. The first and last boss fights are excellent, but the rest of them are mostly fighting trolls, so I think that they aren't that good, except mentioned 2 and one more. Side bosses are a similar story except for Valkyries which are awesome. Took me 50 hours to 100% complete the game on hard, but I've already beaten the game before and I really took my time, so if you only want to focus on the main story with a bit of exploring t shouldn't take you more than 35 hours. If you specifically focus on the main story, you will probably be able to finish it in around 20-25 hours. Performance is okay I guess, it ran well, but not perfect. I had occasional stutters, but they didn't bother me.

[h2] Сюжет игры [/h2]
История Бога Войны рассказывает о сложных отношениях между суровым отцом Кратосом и его неопытным сыном Атреем. Вместе они должны объединиться для общей цели, ведь они последние друг у друга. Сюжет игры намного глубже, чем кажется на первый взгляд, и это хорошо, потому что для меня сюжет — важнейшая составляющая хорошей одиночной видеоигры.

[h2] Про дополнительные квесты [/h2]
В игре их не так много, большинство из них — это небольшие миссии, в которых вы ищете тот или иной предмет. Такой тип дополнительных миссий сопровождается интересными мини-историями, рассказывающими о судьбе того или иного персонажа. Есть и довольно скучные квесты, где вам нужно отправиться в определенное место и устроить там замес, но таких дополнительных миссий всего пара штук.
В побочных заданиях также присутствуют карты сокровищ и сбор коллекционных предметов, которые можно обменять на опыт.

[h2] Геймплей [/h2]
В игре отличная боевая система. В распоряжении игрока боевой топор [i] «Левиафан» [/i], которым очень приятно сражаться, особенно метать его во врагов. По мере прохождения игры можно открывать различные навыки, позволяющие использовать новые атаки и комбинировать их с уже изученными. Аналогично хорошо проработан ближний бой с помощью кулаков и щита. Разнообразие добивающих анимаций для одинаковых мобов хоть и скудное (часто только одна), но выглядят они очень эффектно. Хорошо реализована механика помощи Атрея в бою, который с помощью своего лука помогает нам в сражениях (иногда он просто необходим).
Система прокачки представляет из себя повышение определенных характеристик главного героя с помощью брони, чар и талисманов.

[i] Отдельно хочется отметить режиссуру. Игра происходит в одном кадре, из-за чего переход между геймплеем и кат-сценой ощущается очень плавным. [/i]

[h2] Открытый мир [/h2]
Открытый мир в этой игре впечатляет. Он состоит из нескольких уникальных миров, самый большой из которых — Мидгард. Мидгард состоит из нескольких регионов со своими историями и секретами. Весь мир отлично проработан, можно встретить много завораживающих пейзажей, которые однозначно попадут в вашу библиотеку скриншотов.

[h2] Подведём итоги [/h2]
[h3] Плюсы: [/h3]
+Глубокий сюжет (прохождение основной сюжетной кампании занимает около 25 часов)
+Боевая система
+Открытый мир, который хочется изучать даже после прохождения основной сюжетной кампании
+Относительно легкая платина (потребовалось около 40 часов на средней сложности)
+Звуковое сопровождение
+Оптимизация
[h3] Минусы: [/h3]
-Сюжет может захватить не сразу. Мне потребовалось около 5 часов, чтобы погрузиться
-Присутствует пара скучных дополнительных квестов (скорее недочет, чем минус)

-Однообразные анимации добивания для одинакового типа мобов (скорее недочет, чем минус)

[b] Пройдя этот шедевр полностью, понимаешь, что игра заслуживает всех наград, которые она получила. Я с нетерпением жду [b] God of War: Ragnarök [/b] на пк. [/b]

[b] Introspective (Something Different): [/b]
I want to approach this write up a little differently. You can catch all my technical thoughts about the game above, but I want to take a bit of an introspective look into this game. The fact that I'm doing this is a testament of how good the game is. But I want to look at the themes and how they apply to me and maybe you (the reader) as well. I'm sure that what I will say is nothing new. The game has been out for six years after all.

Immediately we are put into the game with a husband who lost a wife and a son who lost a mother. The difference in demeanor gives you an idea of how these two characters' lives have been to this point. Kratos is what we see in a lot of today's culture among men, young boys, and me. A traditional personality upbringing, "You're a man, you will not cry". Something we have all either heard or personally dealt with. Then you have Atreus. A more sensitive child, vying for the approval of a father he feels is so distant. Losing the parent he felt as though he had more of a connection to he now feels lost. 

Atreus is the child that we've all been and as adults all find somewhat annoying. We can sympathize with doing activities to please a parent. We've all been through a phase of angst. Betrayed with the thought that our youth means we were once invincible. Dealing with the consequences of that ignorance. Lastly, being humbled to the point where we learn how to shake and move with learned wisdom. This is the character arc we see in an accelerated time for Atreus but is relevant in the life I have lived and maybe yourself as well.
This is made more difficult for Kratos because we see throughout the journey that he struggles with his past exploits. This rendition of God of War does not wipe clean the slate of Kratos. It is in fact a plot point that hangs throughout the story and me personally. Understanding as an adult what and how to share with your children when the time calls for it. When leading a family how do you deal or grow through your past exploits. Knowing that in our lives we are far from perfect people, how did you make it through, and possibly keep history from repeating itself. This is a taste of the thoughts a parent goes through. That I know I will go through when raising a child. It’s visible to Kratos when traveling with his son. These actions, decisions, and choices hover because it makes you think to yourself, what is the proper amount of information a child needs to stimulate their growth. Or is it truly detrimental to keep information from them and call it protection?   

All through this process we have Kratos. The hardened warrior, molded by traditional spartan upbringing, raising a child. His child. Not a warrior. He is thrusted into a role unfamiliar to him and must make the conscious decision to be a father and not just a caretaker. Understanding that when disciplining and teaching our children that a subtle hand is sometimes more effective than the deft hand, we're familiar with. 

The bonding that takes place during the adventure leads to not only self-discovery but also discovery of what makes Atreus tick. Fatherhood is a journey. One of fear, self-doubt, and even stupid decisions. It is important though that you continue to make that journey. The journey of Kratos and Atreus saw multiple times where they could have packed up and gone home but teaching a child to see things through builds character and resilience in the face of adversity. Character shapes you into the person you will one day be. For Kratos, and for parents, it is imperative to know how to build that in all our children; so that they become the success that not only we want them to be but the success that they want to see as well. God of War tackles parenthood with an amazing sense of detail in a video game that sometimes you forget that you're ripping and tearing threats limb from limb.

I'm obviously in the minority here, I understand that. I've never given a negative review before. And I've never disliked a game with such raving reviews. But I honestly can't understand such a high review score. Don't get me wrong, the game is made with a high production value. You can see it in the graphics, animations, art style... but there's something just off about it for me. 

For one, while the graphics and art style are very good, I just don't think it fits as well as it should. As a game  set in Norse mythology and culture, it doesn't do the time period justice. I was expecting a gritty, grimy, setting with ancient cities built in stone and magnificent wooden halls... but that's not what this game has to offer. It felt like a carbon copy of assassins creed and the Isu. Much more high fantasy and not dirty, war obsessed gods based on the actual Norse mythology. But mythology is up to subjective interpretation, and maybe it just didn't match MY interpretation of what I expected. 

I have to admit, the game has amazing presentation at onset. I loved this old god living in a hole in the wall shack(more of my interpretation of Norse mythology) attempting to live a life he wants. That part of the story gripped me and I was all for it. Unfortunately, that ended just as fast as it started. And in my opinion, the best combat sequence in the game so far was in the first hour. And it goes all downhill from there. 

The combat seems fun and exciting at first. Throwing the axe was a thrill. But it becomes unbelievably, incredibly stale after a mere hour or 2. Plus, it makes zero sense how Kratos goes from literally throwing mountains in the first big fight, to having to hit the scrawny little undead creatures 15 times to kill them. It doesn't make sense to me. It took me out of the immersion so much. It hurt to see what could be and then be forced to wack at little enemies over and over again in the same manner.

The enemies are extremely repetitive. You rarely fight something you haven't encountered before after the first 2 hours. Maybe a couple reskins here and there. Truly disappointing. The funniest thing about the game is that there is a bestiary. A bestiary. A bestiary in a game with maybe 10 or a couple more enemy types. With barely any variety between them. And it's not like The Witcher where you use the bestiary to study up on an enemy and learn how to defeat them more efficiently. Nah, it's really just here is this enemy. It's in the game. Blows my mind they added a bestiary. Hilarious even. 

The puzzle are horrendous. They aren't puzzles. It's just finding the correct trajectory to fling my axe at a couple bulbous plants that then release a chest or a door. That's it. I mean really. It's honestly it. 

And the chests. Oh god the chests. So many of them. Everywhere. Complete with the same extra long animation that you can't escape. And there's never anything that I care in them. Ever. The only thing you pull out of them are these little leather-looking pouches. No matter what you pull out of that chest, it's gonna be a tiny little pouch half the size of your hand. You can come across a beautifully designed, ornate chest that radiates "open me... I have amazing loot", and it's just 1 tiny pouch that contains some skill, uninteresting crafting component or some god awful talisman or charm. 

The "crafting" and upgrade system are a total slog as well. Terribly integrated into a game about a living god. Why do I need this little piece of armor? I'm a god. I throw mountains at things I don't like. It also completely artificially bumps up play time. I don't want to sit through this game tinkering with a myriad of different armor specs. In some games sure. But it doesn't fit when you are controlling the God of War. 

I see why some people like the game. I do. But it's painfully casual. And that inherently isn't a problem. It's just the game tries to put up this facade of a great, father and son epic, fighting undead and gods alike... but then the gameplay and feel of the game is completely casual. It's a very odd mix that I've never experienced before. 

Also, I swear the only reason the FoV is so ridiculously low, is to hide the son's terrible pathfinding, logic, and frankly amusing teleportation to catch up to you. That's the reason. I'm convinced.

A stunningly beautiful game with characters you grow to love. This is quite the adventure and I was 'all in' within a few minutes of starting. In the midst of Norse mythology, it is a sweet and heartwarming story about a father and a son building a relationship.

For me, it was a tough game, as I don't excel in combat. Thus, I played on the easiest setting which still was challenging.  There is no real penalty for death (just try again) and the explicit save system has dozens of slots.

The fights are relentless... monsters and spirits just keep showing up along your path and you do not have stealth options to avoid them.  I used 'brute-force' combat (charging forth with weapons blazing) and learned a new level of coordination with my keyboard and mouse to control special moves and runic attacks. In between encounters, there are environmental puzzles to solve, scenery to take in, and some tricky moves to open doors and chests. What a journey and I'm sorry to see it end!

You will do a fair bit of climbing and jumping but (at least in easy mode), you can't miss a jump or fall off an edge. This was much appreciated! 

Completionists will need to grind through two extra realms/areas that become accessible towards the end of the game.. Neither added anything to the story (in my opinion) and I slogged through both in search of the associated achievements.

The rest of the game is, in a word, spectacular! Great story, characters, voice acting, cinematics, etc. The game world is huge and diverse and you travel by foot, by boat and (ultimately) by fast travel through mystic gates. There are more collectibles than one can count and it pays to explore every corner of every environment. Resources abound and it was only at the end that I was short on rare items when I was trying to upgrade armor and weapons.

I can't say enough good things about God of War.  If you like 'big' game worlds with a captivating story, like Assassins Creed Origins or Horizon Zero Dawn, then this game is definitely something you will enjoy.

This game is absolutely a modern masterpiece. One of the greatest video game stories told, as well as one of the greatest melee combat systems in gaming. I first played God of War on PS4 back in 2018, and this was actually the first modern, post PS3 Sony exclusive I had played. I loved it then, however, playing it again in 2023 with the added context of Ragnarok, as well as having played the original game and God of War III significantly elevated the experience. I still adored the game when I played it without this context which is absolutely a testament to its quality. I also read a book on Norse Mythology by Neil Gaiman before replaying, which added another layer to the story which was really fascinating. I really enjoyed seeing how the game changed the established myths, while also staying true to their nature. 

My only real complaint is that the difficulty kind of falls apart a bit on the higher settings. Namely enemies getting out of stun from long runic attacks (or not taking any damage from them for some reason) as well as occasionally being completely stunlocked with no way out. Some call the level design shallow and safe, and while I do understand that to some degree, the puzzle dungeon style of design has always been the style of God of War. It is actually kind of remarkable just how similar this game is to the classic games. Just because it has always been the style does not make it good, but I personally like it a lot. I don't really have the game design vocabulary to explain why, but it is easy enough to felicitate constant forward progress with just enough challenge in navigation to make it engaging and satisfying.

To avoid spoiling your enjoyment of the game, I don't want to delve too deeply into the story in this article. All you need to know is that Kratos and Atreus are compelled to climb the highest peak in the Nine Realms for a reason.

God of War is a “complete” game in every sense of the word. What surprises me most is that a series with such a unique main character and action-packed gameplay could produce such a successful game despite taking such a different path. Two features cement this change. The first is the storytelling that brings Kratos and his son's adventure to our screens.

Kratos is not a paragon of perfection. He is a wounded soul who carries the traces of his past life (literally) on his shoulders. When he left one mythological realm behind and arrived in another, his sole aim was to live a quiet, peaceful life. Although he managed to fulfill this wish for a while with his wife Faye and son Atreus, for certain reasons, he finds himself alone with Atreus, with whom he has been unable to establish a father-son relationship. Atreus is a child trained by his mother, who knows how to fend for himself despite his young age. However, his relationship with Kratos consists solely of obeying his orders.

The Song of Blood and Ice

The second defining feature I mentioned above is in the game's combat mechanics. Forget the old games' Kratos with his camera set meters back, and the absurd combat sequences where you kill dozens of enemies at once. The new God of War isn't interested in that. One of the most important features of this game is how it portrays Kratos and Atreus's adventure and the bond between them in the most raw and impactful way possible. To achieve this, the combat mechanics and camera need to be a bit more personal. Now the camera is right behind Kratos, and the fights feel more personal. This personal touch is also supported by the game's “single-take” camera style. After pressing New Game at the start of the game, the camera doesn't cut away during cutscenes or loading screens. The entire game gives you the feeling that you are playing through the eyes of someone witnessing Kratos and Atreus' adventure firsthand. This choice wonderfully supports both the storytelling and the combat mechanics.

About 60% of the game takes place in the mortal realm of Midgard. The remaining portion involves visiting different realms and stepping foot on lands that have become the stuff of legends. I don't want to mention which realms you visit or under what conditions, as for me, the most enjoyable parts of the game were my visits to these realms. But don't expect a massive game area like the one in Midgard from every realm. Without going into too much detail, I can say that the game area in Midgard is detailed and encourages exploration.

The main area you'll find yourself in after the first five hours of the game is packed with challenges, side quests, surprises, and story fragments. Here, you can take on side quests from Brok and Sindri, enter previously inaccessible secret areas, search for loot on stranded ships; chase legends straight out of Norse mythology; or rescue creatures in need of your help. I estimate that doing everything in Midgard would take only about 30 hours.


In my opinion, this game is a masterpiece. I really wanted to play it back when I didn't own a PS4. It's not just about the gameplay; there's a ton of other stuff behind it. The actors, the development process, the overall GoW lore...
But that's a topic for another post :D

I grew up playing the original God Of War games. All of them were fun for the type of games they were. Button mashing mayhem. 

I finally got around to playing this title, and while it's beautiful, well optimized, and has stellar voice acting- That's really all that appealed to me. Sony has adopted a very formulaic system for their exclusives. Uncharted, The Last Of Us, etc. They all "feel" the same to me. 

I'm the minority here, and that's okay. But God Of War as a modern title, lacks innovation in combat and exploration. Everything about the gameplay feels far too conventional. To me, it's a God Of War theme slapped on Sony's Santa Monica engine.

Difficulty settings were simply enemy damage increased, make enemy sponge.

Traversing felt expired. And akin to earlier titles made with the Santa Monica engine. (Go to ledge, press b, automated jump)

Story seems to be something special. I can appreciate the father and son theme. 

Puzzles definitely gave me some nostalgic vibes from the previous GOW titles. 

I can see why people love this. It's gorgeous, controls and movement are smooth, and a compelling story with a different take on God Of War. But the gameplay itself is where it falls apart for me.
